WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- Secretary of State Hillary Clinton reached an important milestone Wednesday in her quest to pay the debt from her failed 2008 presidential bid: For the first time in eight months, her campaign committee reported having more money in the bank than it owes. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's campaign committee reported owing $2.3 million in debt at the end of March. On a day most Americans were preoccupied with filing their federal income taxes, Clinton's campaign committee filed finance documents with the Federal Election Commission, reporting a total of $2.3 million in debts at the end of March, compared with $2.6 million in the bank. The nation's top diplomat has been steadily chipping away at unpaid campaign bills since suspending her White House bid in June 2008, when her debt peaked at $25.2 million. That amount covered $12 million owed to vendors, as well as the $13.2 million she loaned her campaign from personal funds. Clinton's campaign was unable to repay that personal loan by the time the Democratic National Convention convened in Denver, Colorado, last August, the deadline mandated by the 2002 McCain-Feingold campaign finance law. The former New York senator was forced to forgive the entire loan amount. Her campaign owed $6.4 million to 16 creditors at the end of November; $5.9 million to five creditors at the end of December; and the current $2.3 million owed to just one creditor at the end of March. That creditor is Penn, Schoen & Berland, a political consulting and polling firm that advised Clinton during her presidential bid. The firm's president, Mark Penn, was Clinton's senior campaign strategist until he stepped down last April amid revelations that he had lobbied on behalf of Colombia for a U.S.-Colombia trade deal that Clinton opposed. Penn remained involved with the campaign. Earlier this year, Clinton and her supporters raced to pay as much of the debt as possible by the time she was confirmed and sworn in as the nation's 67th secretary of state on January 21. As of that date, Clinton became subject to a federal law known as the Hatch Act, which prohibits federal employees from personally soliciting or accepting political contributions. The Hatch Act allows others to keep raising money on Clinton's behalf, without her direct involvement. This week, longtime Clinton ally James Carville, a CNN contributor, sent a fundraising e-mail to Democrats on behalf of Clinton's campaign, requesting contributions of as little as $5 in exchange for a chance to win one of several prizes, including spending a day with former President Bill Clinton. "I won't spend a lot of time trying to convince you to help Hillary," Carville e-mailed. "I know what she means to you, and I'm sure you know how important it is for her to have her campaign pay off all its obligations." It's unclear whether the campaign will use the $2.6 million in the bank to clear its $2.3 million in debts in the short term. Continued fundraising indicates that it will not. Additional operating expenses and other outlays could emerge. Any extra money from the campaign could be donated to political causes or returned to donors. Clinton's campaign reported raising $938,000 in contributions in the first three months of 2009. In addition to tapping traditional fundraising, the campaign also generated money by selling or renting various campaign assets to other organizations. It received $2.6 million from Clinton's "Friends of Hillary" U.S. Senate campaign committee for the sale of unspecified assets and an additional $2.2 million from renting out its lists of campaign supporters. Organizations that have rented Clinton's lists include the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the inaugural committee of then-President-elect Barack Obama, and the William Jefferson Clinton Foundation. Those organizations each paid $274,297. Clinton's political action committee, HillPAC, rented the lists for $822,492. Among the Democratic candidates who have rented Clinton's campaign lists are Arkansas Sen. Blanche Lincoln; Virginia gubernatorial candidate and former Clinton campaign Chairman Terry McAuliffe; New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who was appointed to fill Clinton's seat; and New York congressional candidate Scott Murphy, who hopes to succeed Gillibrand in the U.S. House.

That creditor is Penn, Schoen & Berland, a political consulting and polling firm that advised Clinton during her presidential campaign. The firm’s president, Mark Penn, served as Clinton’s senior campaign strategist until stepping down last April amid revelations that he had lobbied on Colombia’s behalf for a U.S.-Colombia trade agreement that Clinton opposed. In paperwork submitted to the Federal Election Commission on the same day many Americans were focused on the federal income-tax filing deadline, the committee said it ended March with $2.6 million on hand and $2.3 million still owed.

Clinton has gradually reduced the campaign’s unpaid bills since ending her run for the White House in June 2008. At that time, the debt had climbed to $25.2 million. The total consisted of $12 million due to vendors and $13.2 million that Clinton had personally lent to the campaign.

Under the 2002 McCain-Feingold campaign-finance law, the personal loan had to be repaid before the Democratic National Convention opened in Denver, Colorado, the following August. Because the campaign failed to meet that deadline, the former New York senator had to forgive the full $13.2 million.

The committee’s remaining obligations have fallen sharply. At the end of November, it owed $6.4 million to 16 creditors. By the end of December, that figure had dropped to $5.9 million owed to five creditors. At the close of March, only one creditor remained, with a balance of $2.3 million.

His departure followed disclosures that he had lobbied for Colombia in support of a U.S.-Colombia trade agreement that Clinton opposed. From that date forward, she was covered by the Hatch Act, a federal law barring government employees from personally requesting or receiving political donations. # Clinton campaign reports $2.6 million in cash, $2.3 million in debt

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign committee reported having $2.6 million in cash and $2.3 million in outstanding debt at the end of March 2009, according to a campaign finance filing.

The figures show the committee remained financially active months after Clinton ended her bid for the 2008 Democratic presidential nomination. Although the cash on hand was enough to cover the reported debt on paper, campaign funds may also be needed for administrative expenses and other obligations associated with winding down the operation.

Clinton suspended her campaign in June 2008 after a prolonged primary contest with Barack Obama, who went on to win the presidency. She later joined his administration as secretary of state.

Former presidential campaigns often continue raising and spending money after an election as they settle bills, maintain required records and comply with federal reporting rules. The March filing provides a snapshot of Clinton’s continuing effort to close out the financial side of her historic White House campaign.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how Hillary Clinton paid down the debts from her unsuccessful 2008 presidential campaign after becoming secretary of state, including relevant FEC filings and Hatch Act restrictions.
counterfactuals.output:
Hillary Clinton did not use State Department funds or her secretary-of-state salary to retire her 2008 campaign debt. The debt was handled through her still-active presidential campaign committee, **Hillary Clinton for President, FEC committee C00431569**.

### How the debt was reduced

- Clinton’s campaign ended the 2008 primary season with roughly **$25 million in obligations**, although the total varied by reporting date.
- About **$13 million was money Clinton had personally loaned the campaign**. In late 2008 she forgave most of those loans, converting them into an effective personal contribution and substantially reducing the committee’s reported debt.
- When she became secretary of state in January 2009, approximately **$6 million or more in outside/vendor debt** reportedly remained.
- The committee stayed open and continued accepting lawful, post-election contributions designated to the 2008 primary. Supporters—including Bill Clinton and other political allies—organized appeals and fundraising events. The Obama political network also encouraged donors who had not reached their legal limits to help retire the debt.
- Contributions for debt retirement remained subject to the contribution limits applicable to the **2008 primary election**. A donor who had already contributed the maximum for that election could not simply give again, and the committee could not raise more than its remaining “net debts outstanding.”

### What the FEC filings showed

Because the committee remained active, it continued filing presidential-campaign reports—generally **FEC Form 3P**—after the election:

- Receipts were itemized on **Schedule A**.
- Payments to vendors and fundraising expenses appeared on **Schedule B**.
- Outstanding debts and obligations appeared on **Schedule C**.
- Successive reports showed the debt declining from millions of dollars to a relatively small balance.
- The committee’s **2012 year-end report, filed in January 2013**, reported that the remaining debt had been eliminated. Later filings reflected no campaign debt, although the committee could remain open temporarily to resolve administrative matters and dispose of any remaining cash.

Thus, the FEC record describes a conventional debt-retirement operation: Clinton forgave her own loans, while the committee raised contributions and paid vendors until the debt reached zero.

### Hatch Act restrictions

As secretary of state, Clinton was a covered executive-branch employee under the **Hatch Act**, particularly **5 U.S.C. § 7323(a)**. Among other things, the law prohibited her from:

- using her official authority to affect an election; and
- personally soliciting, accepting, or receiving political contributions.

Accordingly, while serving as secretary she could not personally make fundraising calls, sign solicitations in her official capacity, direct State Department employees to help, use government resources, or appear as the fundraiser at campaign-debt events. The president and vice president have special Hatch Act exemptions, but the secretary of state does not.

The Hatch Act did **not**, however:

- erase the old campaign’s debts;
- require the campaign committee to close;
- prevent the committee from receiving lawful debt-retirement contributions; or
- prevent Bill Clinton, campaign staff, or private supporters from raising money independently of her official duties.

The FEC regulated the reporting, contribution limits, and debt accounting. Hatch Act compliance was principally within the jurisdiction of the **U.S. Office of Special Counsel**, not the FEC. In practical terms, the arrangement was designed to keep Clinton herself out of fundraising while allowing her private campaign committee and supporters to finish paying the 2008 obligations.

counterfactuals.output:
# Clinton’s 2008 Campaign Used Fundraising, Asset Sales and List Rentals to Erase Its Debt

**WASHINGTON —** Hillary Rodham Clinton’s unsuccessful 2008 presidential campaign took nearly five years to close its books, relying on post-election fundraising, the sale of campaign property and paid access to its valuable supporter list to eliminate millions of dollars owed to vendors.

When Clinton ended her Democratic primary campaign in June 2008, her committee reported debts exceeding $20 million. A large share consisted of money Clinton had lent the campaign herself—roughly $13 million—while the remainder was owed to pollsters, consultants, printers, travel companies and other vendors.

Clinton later forgave the personal loans, meaning she would not be repaid. That decision substantially reduced the committee’s formal obligations but left several million dollars in commercial debt that federal election law still required the campaign to report and settle.

By early 2013, Federal Election Commission filings showed that the remaining vendor debt had been paid, allowing the committee to wind down.

## Fundraising continued after the primary

The debt-reduction effort began soon after Clinton conceded the nomination to Barack Obama.

As part of the Democratic Party’s effort to unite after the bitter primary, Obama appeared with Clinton at a June 2008 fundraising event in Washington. Clinton’s supporters were urged to back Obama in the general election, while Obama donors were encouraged to help retire Clinton’s outstanding obligations. Obama himself made a contribution to Clinton’s debt-retirement effort.

Bill Clinton also helped raise money through appeals and events. The campaign continued soliciting former donors, often emphasizing that unpaid vendors—not Clinton personally—would benefit from the contributions after she forgave her loans.

Those appeals faced an important legal limitation after Clinton became secretary of state in January 2009. Cabinet officials are restricted from partisan political fundraising, so Clinton could not personally conduct the kind of aggressive donor outreach normally used to pay down a campaign debt. Former aides, political allies and Bill Clinton took a more visible role, while the campaign committee remained active largely for debt-retirement and administrative purposes.

The committee also used standard direct-mail and online techniques, including small-dollar appeals and fundraising promotions tied to meetings or events with Bill Clinton.

## Campaign property was converted into cash

Like other committees that end a national campaign, Clinton’s organization liquidated property that was no longer needed. Campaign assets—including office equipment, computers, furniture and other materials—could be sold, with the proceeds deposited in the campaign account and used to pay lawful obligations.

The most valuable property, however, was not office furniture. It was the campaign’s political database: the names, email addresses and other information associated with millions of donors, volunteers and supporters accumulated during the 2008 race.

Federal rules generally allow a campaign to sell or rent such assets if the transaction is conducted at fair-market value and properly disclosed. Paying less than market value could amount to an illegal or unreported contribution; paying a commercially reasonable price turns the transaction into income for the committee that owns the list.

## The supporter list became a major revenue source

Clinton’s list had enduring value because it identified a large national pool of politically engaged Democrats—many of whom had donated online, volunteered or expressed interest in her candidacy.

The campaign rented access to that list to other Democratic political organizations and campaigns. President Obama’s 2012 reelection operation was among the most significant users, paying substantial sums for access to Clinton’s supporters. FEC reports and contemporaneous accounts placed the Obama campaign’s list-related payments in the seven figures.

The arrangement benefited both sides. Obama’s campaign obtained access to a Democratic audience outside its own database, while Clinton’s dormant presidential committee received revenue it could use to pay old bills.

A list rental did not necessarily mean that Clinton’s committee permanently surrendered ownership of the data. In a typical political list transaction, the renter receives permission to send a specified number or type of messages. The owner may continue to control and rent the list later.

The arrangement nonetheless raised questions among some supporters who did not expect information supplied to one campaign to become a revenue-producing asset. Such rentals are common in political fundraising, however, and are permissible when they comply with campaign-finance rules and the committee’s privacy commitments.

## The debt fell gradually

The headline debt figure attached to Clinton’s 2008 campaign can be misleading because it included her personal loans. At the end of the primary, the campaign’s total obligations were above $20 million, but forgiving approximately $13 million in candidate loans removed more than half of that burden without producing cash for vendors.

The remaining outside debt—several million dollars—was reduced over the following years through:

- contributions from Clinton and Democratic supporters;
- fundraisers organized by allies;
- direct-mail and online appeals;
- sales of physical campaign property;
- rental or sale of campaign-related assets, especially the supporter database; and
- negotiated payments to vendors.

By late 2012, only a small amount remained. Early in 2013, the committee reported that it had retired the final obligations from the 2008 race.

## Political significance

The long payoff period illustrated both the financial damage caused by the extended 2008 Democratic primary and the continuing value of the organization Clinton built during it.

It also preserved relationships with consultants and vendors whose services could matter in a future campaign. Leaving bills unpaid can harm a candidate’s standing with political professionals; paying them, even years later, helped Clinton close the 2008 contest without carrying a formal campaign debt into her next phase of national politics.

The database that helped erase the debt later became important for another reason: it represented part of the organizational foundation for renewed efforts to promote Clinton as a presidential candidate. Outside groups seeking to build support for a possible 2016 campaign also pursued access to Clinton-aligned voter and donor information, though those later arrangements were separate from the principal debt-retirement transactions of the 2008 committee.

In the end, Clinton did not recover the millions she had personally advanced. Instead, she wrote off those loans, while the campaign used conventional fundraising and the commercial value of its remaining assets—most notably its supporter list—to ensure that outside creditors were paid.

## Clinton Campaign’s Cash Finally Exceeds Its Debt

**WASHINGTON —** For the first time in eight months, Hillary Rodham Clinton’s 2008 presidential campaign reported having more money in the bank than it owed, marking a modest financial turnaround for an operation that ended the Democratic primary deeply in debt.

According to its latest federal campaign-finance filing, Hillary Clinton for President had approximately **$5.9 million in cash on hand** and about **$5.4 million in outstanding debts and obligations**. The roughly half-million-dollar surplus was the campaign’s first positive cash-to-debt balance since the closing months of the 2008 Democratic nomination contest.

Clinton’s campaign accumulated millions of dollars in bills as it battled Barack Obama through the final primaries in June 2008. The obligations included unpaid invoices to consultants, pollsters and other vendors. The largest creditor was longtime Clinton strategist **Mark Penn’s firm**, which was still owed several million dollars.

The campaign’s overall financial picture had once been substantially worse. Clinton personally lent her presidential committee **$13.2 million** during the primary race, but later forgave that loan, removing it from the committee’s outstanding debt. The campaign also benefited from fundraising assistance after Clinton endorsed Obama and appeared with him at events intended in part to help her retire the remaining bills.

Another source of revenue was the campaign’s extensive donor and supporter lists. Political committees can rent such lists to other organizations while retaining ownership of the data. Federal filings showed list-rental arrangements involving organizations including **Obama for America** and the **Democratic National Committee**, both of which sought access to Clinton’s large network of Democratic donors and activists.

The improved balance sheet did not mean the campaign had finished paying its creditors. Millions remained due, and much of the cash on hand was expected to be used for that purpose. Still, after months in which liabilities exceeded available funds, the filing represented the clearest sign yet that Clinton’s presidential committee was moving toward eliminating the debt left by the long 2008 primary campaign.
